Usage ledger

The gateway also appends one content-free row per finished request to <state>/usage/usage-YYYY-MM.jsonl (UTC month). The directory is mode 0700 and the files 0600. The current month and the previous 12 are kept; older files are removed on the first write and whenever the month changes. Set GATEWAY_USAGE_LEDGER=off to disable it: nothing is created, imported or marked. It is independent of GATEWAY_TELEMETRY.

A row holds only v, at, host, requestId, responseId (marked responses only), provider, providerType, model, status (completed, empty or failed), origin (gateway, or telemetry for imported rows), session (imported rows only), inputTokens (gross, including cached), cachedTokens, cacheWriteTokens, outputTokens, reasoningTokens, nanoAiu and nanoAiuStatus. nanoAiu is Copilot's credit amount in billionths of a credit; null means none was reported, which is not zero. nanoAiuStatus is present on every Copilot row that has usage: complete when every model call of the request was priced, partial when only some were priced or Copilot itself called a figure partial (the amount is then a floor), and unavailable when none was. A request that fails after a provider reported usage keeps that usage, and so does a request whose caller disconnected after the provider reported it, so a Copilot call that is billed and then rejected or abandoned still shows up. When a request stops early (the caller left, it was cancelled or timed out, or the gateway is shutting down), even while the gateway waits for a slow client to take earlier output, the server reads the provider on for up to 3 seconds, for usage only, so usage the provider received before the stop is not lost. At shutdown the server waits for those requests to write their rows before it flushes telemetry and the ledger, but a stopping process leaves 1.5 seconds after the drain deadline at the latest. Before it leaves, it records every request still running as failed (a ledger row and a request_failed event with abortCause shutdown) with the usage received so far, and then flushes both, so usage that arrives later than that is not recorded but usage already received is. A row with no tokens and no credit amount is not written.

Never stored: prompts, instructions, messages, tool names, arguments or outputs, images, thread, session or turn ids, account ids, credentials, error text or environment values.

Marker. For copilot-subscription and claude-subscription routes, while the ledger is on, the Responses id is resp_gl_<request id without dashes> instead of a random resp_<hex>. Codex records that id in its own rollout, so a spend tool counts a gateway request once, from the ledger, and skips the matching Codex record. A Messages request on those routes gets the message id msg_gl_<request id without dashes> instead of a random msg_<hex>, and its row records that id. Claude Code records that msg_gl_ id in its transcripts, so a spend tool that dedupes transcript records by id sees the same id the ledger holds. A consumer must accept both prefixes (resp_gl_ and msg_gl_; the gatewayMarkerPrefixes list in src/usage-ledger.ts), not only resp_gl_, or it counts Messages requests twice.

Telemetry import. The first time the ledger is prepared, and <state>/usage/telemetry-import.json is absent, each request_* telemetry event with input or output tokens becomes one origin: "telemetry" row (no response id), and the marker file records the count. This keeps request history that telemetry would drop after its 14 days. An imported row keeps the cache-write, reasoning and credit figures its event carries (cacheWriteTokens, reasoningTokens, nanoAiu, nanoAiuStatus); an event from before those fields existed has none, so its row reads 0 for the token figures and null for nanoAiu. providerType is set only for providers in the current configuration. The import skips every request this process records and any request already in the ledger, and writes in one append per month, so a request is never counted twice; a reader also keeps one row per request id and prefers the gateway's own row over an imported one.

gateway diagnostics also sums Copilot credits per model from nanoAiu.

Running component releases

An install only moves the current link, so a process that started earlier keeps running the release it loaded. Its command line can still say .../current/..., which no longer identifies that code after an install. Managed releases keep a read-only descriptor for their immutable CLI entrypoint and release marker, so lsof can preserve that release during installer cleanup even when the app-owned Node itself only names current. A hot-swapped server retains each old marker only until that generation's requests drain. gateway versions [--json] [--check] answers that question: it lists this user's gateway processes, names each one's role (service, inference, desktop-adapter, ssh-listener, ssh-proxy, executor-host, gateway-engine, native-relay, tunnel or other) and reads the release from mapped files found with lsof. For CLI roles, it reads all descriptors for that same PID and accepts only one open immutable releases/V/package/dist/cli.js entry beneath this install root. A floating current launch path is never evidence: if the immutable CLI descriptor cannot be read, the release is unknown unless the process was launched directly from one unambiguous immutable release path. A release marker alone does not prove the bootstrap release, because an older CLI can hot-load a newer server generation and retain its marker. It rechecks the PID and its start time after reading descriptors, dropping a row if that process exited or its PID was reused during the scan. The report skips this process itself, so running the command never adds a row.

For the service, gateway health instead uses the optional runningRelease published by that service at startup. It accepts the release only when the status names the live service PID and was published after that process started. This keeps an older JavaScript service visible after an install even with an app-owned Node. Older services without the field retain the inventory fallback until they restart on a release that publishes it.

A command line is only read where the program sits: at argv[0], or at argv[1] behind a node interpreter for the CLI script. A wrapper that merely mentions one of our paths inside a quoted string (zsh -c node .../current/package/dist/cli.js serve), a wrapper program such as /usr/bin/time that starts node, another product's releases/ folder, or one of our paths used as an argument, runs none of ours and is left out. Short-lived helper scripts a request starts (such as the Claude tool helper) are not listed. The install root is matched both as written and with its links resolved, so a tree reached through a symlink is still recognized.

The one exception is the inference process. A release that replaced itself in place keeps the node runtime it started with mapped, so lsof names the release it started from rather than the code it serves. There the health endpoint answers instead, and its X-Gateway-Release header wins: the command asks lsof which loopback ports the process listens on, and sends one GET http://127.0.0.1:PORT/health with a two second timeout to each in turn, lowest port first, until one answers. The port comes from the process's own listening socket, never from its arguments, so a server started with a quoted configuration path and no --port is still found. When nothing answers, the report falls back to the mapped release. Those requests are the only thing here that leaves the process, and they never leave the machine.

What is printed is limited to roles, pids, start times and release versions; command arguments, paths and environment values are never shown. A release that neither lsof nor the command line can name reads unknown, and a process started from a source checkout reads checkout. The human form prints the installed release, one row per process with its start time on the local clock, then a summary: all on RELEASE or N lagging: role@release, one mention per distinct pair. --json prints the same data as { installed, processes: [{ role, pid, startedAt, release }], lagging }, where installed is the release the current link points at and startedAt is that start time as a UTC instant. A run from a checkout or worktree, which has no current of its own, names the release the default install's link points at, ~/.local/share/subscription-gateway, and still calls its own processes checkout. When neither link resolves, installed is null, which --json always prints.

--check exits 1 when a process runs another release than the installed one, or unknown, and 0 when none does. It exits 2 when there is no installed release to compare against, because a run that names none cannot tell a lagging process from an up to date one; the report itself is still printed. A flag outside --json and --check, and a process list ps cannot read, exit 2 too; --help or -h prints the usage line and exits 0. See release for how long a lagging process may legitimately take to move.

Exception reports

Staged native executor adoption records native_sharing_staged, native_sharing_activated, and native_sharing_deferred. Records carry only fixed mode or reason codes. A deferral means the staged change was not applied and the current service plan remains authoritative, for example because an old writer remained, the plan changed, or the SDK could not be verified. It does not report a failed chat or authorize replaying a turn. See travel recovery.

Only exceptions go to errors.applifyer.com, project harness-gateway. The DSN is the 1Password item GlitchTip DSN - harness-gateway (vault applifyer) and lives on each Mac in <state>/glitchtip.dsn (mode 0600, owned by the user); a file other users can read is ignored. Without it nothing is sent.

Source Sent as
Uncaught exception or rejection in the server, adapter or service fatal, written synchronously to <state>/error-spool/ and sent by the next process start
Untyped provider failure (provider_failed), internal adapter RPC failure, adapter start failure, execution host start failure error, sent in the background with a five-second timeout
A live Copilot session's own bookkeeping failing: copilot_live_attach (placing a request in its session raised something other than a provider failure; the request is served one-shot), copilot_live_close (closing a session or reporting its end failed), copilot_live_abort (ending a cancelled request failed) error, sent in the background like the row above

Typed provider and protocol failures (including malformed stream frames and invalid historical tool arguments), cancellations and turn anomalies stay in the local log. JSON parser messages are replaced with "JSON parse failed", because they quote the text they failed on. Crash reports are written to a temporary file and renamed, and a spool file that cannot be read is discarded. Events carry the exception type, a scrubbed message (credentials, long secrets, home paths and URL paths removed) and file, function and line frames. The machine is a hashed label; no user, request, environment, device or local variables are sent. Repeats of one failure within ten minutes are dropped, and a process sends at most 30 reports an hour. Set GATEWAY_ERROR_REPORTS=off to disable reporting.
